newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia army to cede jungle to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Colombia army to cede jungle to rebels.

text.p: Thousands of troops will start pulling out of a huge swathe of Colombia's southern jungle at midnight on Thursday (0500 GMT Friday) -- the first time the army has ceded such a large area to the country's leftist guerrillas.

The 32-day demilitarization, which President Ernesto Samper ordered this week, is designed to permit Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas to hand back 60 soldiers they captured almost nine months ago.

Gen. Agustin Ardila, commander of the army's Fourth Division supervising the operation across a 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) area of Caqueta province, said the pull-out would be difficult but ruled out any FARC attack on the estimated 5,000 retreating troops.
"This withdrawal will be difficult. I need about 100 helicopter hours using the (Russian) Mi-17s. We will pull other troops out by land and river," Ardila told Reuters in a phone interview.
"There's no danger in this operation. I have complete control of the area. These narco-bandits have withdrawn deep into the jungle and are too cowardly to face the army," he added.

Ardila said a so-far unspecified number of national and international observers would guarantee that the FARC respected the rules of the temporary demilitarization and did not destroy military bases or place landmines in the zone.
FARC commanders have issued no official communique regarding the demilitarization.

But a rebel source told Reuters earlier this week that "if everything Samper says is true I suppose this could work." He said 10 marines seized by the FARC in fighting in northwest Choco province in January would be released at the same time.

Troops in Caqueta were confined to base for 10 days in December in a bid to persuade the FARC to release the captive soldiers, seized when rebels overran a base in neighbouring Putumayo province on Aug. 30 -- the start of one of the bloodiest offensives in Colombia's three-decade-old guerrilla war.
The FARC, Colombia's largest guerrilla army set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, declined to free their prisoners, arguing the area had not been fully demilitarized.

International Committee of the Red Cross chief Cornelio Sommaruga said Thursday he believed the release of the soldiers would be a "serious evolution" on the road to forging a peace process in Colombia.

But Bogota-based political analyst Alvaro Camacho dismissed such optimism, saying: "This is not the first step on the way to a peace process but it is a chance for the two sides to talk which they haven't done for a long time."
